newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian govt to face more pressure over FX swaps.
newsitem.headline: Belgian govt to face more pressure over FX swaps.

text.p: Belgium's main opposition party said on Tuesday it would pressure the government for more information on a series of botched foreign exchange contracts that could cost the country more than 33 billion Belgian francs.
"It is unacceptable that you cannot give us this information," Rik Daems of the Flemish liberal party VLD told a parliamentary committee meeting with Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt.
"This is about responsibility for speculative decisions, which we cannot judge without a complete dossier," Daems said.

Maystadt said he was willing to assume political responsibility for errors made by Treasury officials and offered the committee a greater say in controlling future operations on Belgium's 10,000 billion Belgian franc debt.
But he declined to give more details about the operations than contained in a 13-page note setting out when positions were built up and their possible cost if closed tomorrow.

"We are at the limit of the information we can give without compromising the Treasury. I will not give the amounts or the names of the counterparties...this would cost the Treasury billions," Maystadt said.
"The amount of the potential loss can only be estimated... the Treasury has put in place a number of measures, which should mean (the situation) can only get better," he added.
According to the note, prepared by the Treasury, the foreign exchange swap and option operations at the centre of the scandal took place in two phases.

In the first, between November 1989 and April 1992, the Treasury built up a book of some 36 swap positions. In the second, between June 1992 and October 1993, the Treasury carried out more swaps aimed at restructuring the earlier transactions and bought a number of options contracts.

The potential loss on the outstanding positions, which mature between 1997 and 2002, would be 33.5 billion Belgian francs at maturity, or 32.6 billion francs, if they were closed tomorrow based on today's interest rates and exchange rates, according to the note.
In addition, a loss of 5.3 billion francs has already been incurred due to the cost of some of the operations, it said.
Maystadt said neither he nor Treasury Director Gregoire Brouhns were informed in detail of the transactions until October 1993, when Belgium's public accounts office was also notified.
But he noted other debt management operations carried out since 1990 had enabled the Treasury to save some 70 billion Belgian francs a year.

"It is impossible to avoid risk in finance...indeed, without taking a risk, it would be impossible to reduce our debt. But it goes without saying this risk should be limited, measured and controlled," Maystadt said.
He offered to discuss Belgium's debt management further when the country unveils a new benchmark portfolio debt management tool next month.
He suggested setting up a new committee composed of members of parliament, representatives of the Treasury and of the public accounts office to regularly review debt operations.
